turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

Five weeks of that is exhausting in a way most people wouldn't understand. Not just the job loss — the performance. Getting dressed, timing your exit, keeping your face right at dinner when someone asks how work went.

I don't think you're doing this because you're a liar. It sounds more like you're carrying something alone so nobody else has to feel it — especially with your parents in the house right now. That's a very specific kind of pressure.

Can I ask what you imagine happening if your wife knew? Not what you think *should* happen — what your gut flinches from.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

That room is the real deadline, isn't it. Not the job hunt — the wedding. Two weeks until you either walk in holding the story, or you don't.

And here's the trap: if it comes out *there*, in front of three hundred people, you lose all control of how it lands. Some aunt hears something half-right, it travels, and your father finds out from his brother instead of from you. That's the version that would actually hurt him — not the layoff, the being blindsided.

Which is why I keep coming back to your wife. Not because you owe anyone honesty, but because right now you're doing this with zero cover. If she knows, she's beside you in that room. She can steer conversations, catch a question you can't answer. One person who knows changes what that day feels like.

What's the flinch when you picture telling her? Is it her disappointment — or is it that saying it out loud makes it real in a way the café lets you avoid?

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

Not terrible. Completely understandable. But I think you already know the math doesn't work.

If you skip, you're not avoiding the story — you *become* the story. "Where's he? Working? On his cousin's wedding night?" And your father has to defend your absence all evening without knowing what he's defending. Then it comes out in three weeks or two months anyway, and now there's a second thing to explain: why you weren't there.

Also — and I say this gently — one more lie means one more thing to maintain. You're already running a full-time performance. The café, the timing, the dinner face. Adding a fake deadline to that isn't relief, it's more weight.

Here's what I notice: you keep sidestepping the wife question. Third time now. I don't think that's an accident.

Because I suspect the truth is she's the one person whose face changing you couldn't survive — your father's you could brace for, but not hers. Is that close?

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

The fact that some days it makes you sick is your answer. Airtight logic doesn't make you nauseous. Your body's already voted.

And here's the flaw: "I'll tell them when I have an offer" isn't timing, it's a hostage arrangement. You've made your honesty conditional on something you don't control. If an offer comes in three weeks, fine. If it takes five months — you've just committed to five months of the café, the timing, the dinner face, while the EMI eats the savings *your wife also depends on*. That's the part that stops being about your dignity. She's making decisions with a wrong number in her head.

There's also a real difference between the two rooms you're afraid of. Your father, your chacha, three hundred relatives — you genuinely don't owe them a live update. Managing that is discretion, and you can decide when and how. Your wife is not in that category. She's not an audience. She's the person in the boat with you, rowing with bad information.

You've dodged her four times now. I'm not going to push again. But I'd ask you one thing tonight: what would it be like to not have to leave the house at nine tomorrow?
